Preterist
prĕt´ẽr-ĭst
n. and adj. (one holding that the prophecies of Matthew 24 and much of Revelation were fulfilled in the first century)
Latin praeteritus, gone by, past. The school takes its name from where it locates the fulfilment: behind us.

Biblical Definition

Preterism holds that the Olivet discourse and much of Revelation were fulfilled in the events of AD 66–70, when Jerusalem fell and the temple was destroyed. Its two pillars are time-texts. The Lord said, “Verily I say unto you, This generation shall not pass, till all these things be fulfilled” (Mat 24:34), having predicted of the temple, “There shall not be left here one stone upon another, that shall not be thrown down” (Mat 24:2); and Luke's version replaces the abomination with an army: “when ye shall see Jerusalem compassed with armies, then know that the desolation thereof is nigh” (Luk 21:20). Revelation twice states its own urgency: “things which must shortly come to pass” (Rev 1:1; Rev 22:6).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines preterite as past; gone by; applied to the tense in grammar which expresses an action or being perfectly past or finished.

expand to see more

PRETERIT, a. Past; applied to the tense in grammar which expresses an action or being perfectly past or finished.

PRETERITION, n. The act of passing by; a passing over or omission.

Key Scripture

Mat 24:34 — "Verily I say unto you, This generation shall not pass, till all these things be fulfilled."

Mat 24:2 — "And Jesus said unto them, See ye not all these things? verily I say unto you, There shall not be left here one stone upon another, that shall not be thrown down."

Luk 21:20 — "And when ye shall see Jerusalem compassed with armies, then know that the desolation thereof is nigh."

Rev 1:1 — "The Revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave unto him, to shew unto his servants things which must shortly come to pass; and he sent and signified it by his angel unto his servant John:"

Rev 22:6 — "And he said unto me, These sayings are faithful and true: and the Lord God of the holy prophets sent his angel to shew unto his servants the things which must shortly be done."

Modern Corruption

Partial and full preterism are treated as one position, and the second denies a future bodily return and is outside the creeds.

expand to see more

The distinction that must be kept is between partial and full preterism. The partial preterist holds that Matthew 24 and much of Revelation were fulfilled in AD 70, and that the bodily return of Christ, the general resurrection and the last judgment remain future; that view is held by orthodox men across the Reformed tradition and is a question of interpretation. Full or consistent preterism holds that all prophecy, including the second coming and the resurrection, was fulfilled in the first century; that is not an interpretive variation but a denial of an article of the creed, and it puts its holders where Hymenaeus and Philetus stood, saying that the resurrection is past already (2Ti 2:18).

The strength of the position is that it takes the time-texts seriously, and its opponents often do not. This generation shall not pass is a difficulty for every futurist reading, and the attempts to make generation mean race, or the generation that sees the signs, are strained. Equally, the preterist has to account for language in the same discourse that has never plainly happened — the sun darkened, the powers of heaven shaken, the Son of man coming in the clouds with power and great glory — and the apocalyptic-imagery answer, though not unreasonable, has to be applied consistently or it becomes a way of dissolving whatever is inconvenient.

The pastoral corruption of every prophetic school is the same: a system so satisfying that it becomes the lens for the newspaper and eventually for the Bible. The Lord's own application of the discourse is not a chart but a posture — watch therefore, for ye know neither the day nor the hour — and any scheme, preterist or futurist, that leaves a man less watchful has failed the passage it claims to explain.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek genea (G1074), generation; en tachei (G5034), shortly, speedily; eggus (G1451), at hand, near; eremosis (G2050), desolation.

expand to see more

Greek genea (G1074) — generation; Matthew 24:34, 23:36, 12:39, Luke 21:32.

Greek en tachei (G5034) — shortly, speedily; Revelation 1:1, 22:6, Romans 16:20.

Greek eremosis (G2050) — desolation; Matthew 24:15, Luke 21:20, Daniel 9:27 in the Greek.

Usage

"“This generation shall not pass, till all these things be fulfilled” — the text every other school must answer."

"“When ye shall see Jerusalem compassed with armies” — Luke's plainer version."

"“Saying that the resurrection is past already” — where full preterism ends."
